topic: The Behavioral Economics Study That Proves Willpower Doesn't Save Money

sections.voiceover: Here's what the behavioral economics study that proves willpower doesn't save money actually looks like. And it's not what you'd expect.

sections.voiceover:
A real 1998 field experiment (Save More Tomorrow / 'SMarT') at a midwestern manufacturer proved that pre-committing future raises to savings beats asking people to save more today by a massive margin: only 28% accepted an immediate savings increase, but 78% agreed to a future, automatic one — and those who joined nearly quadrupled their savings rate from 3.5% to 13.6% of income within 40 months, with 78% still enrolled after four pay raises. The lesson for viewers: savings challenges and willpower-based budgeting fail for the same reason immediate raises failed — automate the decision once instead of re-deciding every week.. To understand why, you need to see how this actually works.

Save More Tomorrow (SMarT) was designed by Richard Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi and field-tested in 1998 at a midwestern manufacturing company. Employees were offered a plan that increased their 401(k) contribution by 3 percentage points automatically at every future pay raise, capped at 14%.

When offered an immediate increase to their savings rate, only 28% of employees accepted. When offered the same eventual increase but tied to future raises instead, 78% of the employees who had declined the immediate offer agreed to join.

Each of these elements connects. And the connections are what make this story worth telling.

sections.voiceover:
Now here's where it gets interesting.

Employees who joined the SMarT plan raised their average savings rate from 3.5% of income to 13.6% of income over roughly 40 months (four pay raises), and 78% of participants were still enrolled at that point rather than opting out.

Look at this. A Case Western Reserve University study of automated round-up/micro-savings apps found the tools do measurably boost account balances for many users, but the researchers found the benefit is not universal: users without an existing budgeting mindset see meaningfully smaller gains, meaning automation amplifies intent rather than replacing it entirely.

When you see it laid out like this, the pattern is obvious.
